China's First HUMANOID Robot Just Built Itself, XPeng IRON Walks Off the Line #news #technology #china #robot  This is the moment a humanoid robot stopped being assembled by people and started being manufactured like a car. XPeng just switched on the world's first automated production line built for high order humanoid robots, and its flagship robot, IRON, completed final assembly and walked off the line on its own power. No teleoperation, no manual guidance, just a machine finishing itself. IRON runs on three Turing AI chips delivering twenty two hundred fifty TOPS of onboard compute, seventy six degrees of freedom through its body, and twenty one in a single hand alone, numbers that put it ahead of anything else currently shipping in the humanoid robotics space. More than eighty percent of the core manufacturing process is now automated, built on the same car grade consistency standards XPeng already uses for its electric vehicles. Mass production starts by the end of this year, beginning inside XPeng's own stores and campuses, with a full commercial launch across China and international markets targeted for twenty twenty seven. The robotics division just closed a funding round worth more than nine hundred million dollars at a valuation north of six point three billion dollars, the largest single raise any Chinese humanoid robotics company has landed. If you want to see what a scaled, mass produced humanoid robot actually looks like before it reaches the rest of the world, this is it. XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.
